title: How Connected Campus Data Can Improve Energy and Maintenance Decisions
summary: Better visibility into campus data can help schools manage energy, plan maintenance and measure progress against operational goals.
body_markdown:
Sustainability is no longer a standalone initiative for education institutions. It shapes governance, capital planning, risk management and long-term campus strategy. As expectations around environmental, social and governance (ESG) priorities, operational efficiency and reporting grow, schools need a clearer view of how their campuses are performing. That starts with data.


That was one of the clearest messages from our recent webinar with experts across education, sustainability, building performance and connected technologies: schools cannot manage what they cannot see. Whether the goal is reducing energy consumption, improving asset performance, enhancing occupant comfort or preparing for future reporting requirements, better decisions depend on reliable data.


### Sustainability Has Moved Beyond Facilities


For many schools, sustainability was once focused primarily on environmental initiatives and curriculum outcomes. Today, the conversation has evolved.


Educational institutions are increasingly embedding sustainability considerations into infrastructure upgrades, master planning, budgeting decisions and governance frameworks. ESG considerations are becoming part of a broader discussion around risk, resilience, long-term financial planning and future campus development.


At the same time, schools face questions from their communities, insurers and funding partners about how they are putting sustainability into practice. Those conversations can shape decisions about funding and future campus development, bringing sustainability into focus well beyond the facilities team.


The result is a shift from asking, “Should we focus on sustainability?” to “How do we put it into practice?”


### The Hidden Challenge: Limited Visibility


Many schools may already generate the required operational data, but often lack a clear view of it.


Many education campuses operate across multiple buildings, often with a mix of new and ageing infrastructure. HVAC systems, lighting, electrical assets, irrigation systems, water infrastructure and building management systems frequently operate independently from one another.


When those systems are disconnected, facilities teams can struggle to see where performance is slipping, where faults are emerging or where operating costs are rising. The result can be reactive maintenance, unnecessary callouts and missed opportunities to improve performance.


When visibility is limited, even simple questions become difficult to answer:


- Which buildings use the most energy?
- Which assets are approaching end-of-life?
- Where are maintenance resources being spent?
- Which systems are contributing to occupant comfort issues?
- What projects could make the biggest difference to energy and operational performance?


### Connecting the Data Schools Already Have


The good news is that many schools are already generating valuable data across their campus systems.


By connecting building systems, meters and operational technologies into a central platform, schools can begin transforming raw information into data that supports better decisions.


Depending on system configuration and data quality, connected technologies can help schools:


- Monitor energy performance across buildings and campuses
- Identify equipment faults earlier
- Benchmark asset performance
- Track indoor environmental conditions
- Detect anomalies such as power issues or water leaks
- Understand energy consumption patterns and identify potential opportunities for savings


Operational data can also help teams narrow down the source of faults more quickly, potentially reducing the need for repeated site investigation and extended troubleshooting.


### Moving from Reactive to Predictive Maintenance


One of the most significant opportunities for education institutions is shifting from reactive maintenance to proactive asset management.


Schools can manage thousands of assets across their campuses. Yet some organisations still make replacement and investment decisions only after failures occur.


A connected approach can help facilities teams better understand asset condition, performance trends and lifecycle requirements. This creates an opportunity to prioritise upgrades strategically, rather than simply reacting to equipment breakdowns.


For example, an ageing HVAC system may represent more than a maintenance concern. Depending on the selected equipment, building conditions and controls, usage patterns and energy source, an upgrade may improve energy efficiency, reduce emissions, lower operational costs and improve occupant comfort.


With a clearer view of how their assets are performing, schools can make confident investment decisions and direct their capital budgets where they’re needed most.


### Why Measurement Matters


Data alone is not enough. Schools also need a framework for understanding performance and tracking progress.


Sustainability measurement frameworks provide a simple way to translate complex operational data into meaningful benchmarks. Rather than relying solely on annual reviews or isolated performance checks, schools can establish continuous visibility into performance trends and improvement opportunities.


Clear benchmarks also improve communication across stakeholders.


Facilities teams, sustainability managers, business leaders and school executives may all interpret technical information differently. Measurement frameworks provide a common language that helps align decision-making and prioritisation across the organisation.


### Start Small, but Start Now


A recurring theme throughout the discussion was that schools do not need to solve everything at once.


Many institutions are understandably concerned about competing priorities, limited budgets and resource constraints. However, waiting for perfect information can delay meaningful progress.


Instead, schools should focus on establishing a baseline.


This could include:


- Conducting an asset audit
- Understanding utility consumption patterns
- Identifying key energy-consuming systems
- Gathering information on HVAC, electrical, water and building assets
- Creating a central source of truth for operational data


Once that foundation is in place, schools can assess and prioritise improvements based on their risk, expected benefits and available resources, and build a roadmap that aligns with their sustainability, operational and financial objectives.


### The Connected Campus Opportunity


As education institutions prepare for the future, connecting campus systems and operational data can support measurement and informed sustainability planning.


Data-driven asset management can help schools gain visibility into operations, improve maintenance practices, enhance occupant experiences and make informed investment decisions. It can also help institutions track progress against operational and sustainability objectives.


Schools that can turn data into decisions, and decisions into action, will be better positioned to succeed, regardless of whether they have the newest buildings or largest budgets.


Because when it comes to building resilient, efficient and future-ready campuses, visibility is the first step towards transformation.
